where: Section 2 (direct conversion), sentence 'There is no image at a non-zero IF, because the wanted signal is at DC'
problem: The wording is confusing and can be read as 'a zero-IF receiver has no image problem at all'. In a zero-IF receiver the image frequency is fRF itself (the mirror at negative frequency), so the image coincides with the wanted channel; this is exactly why quadrature (I and Q) downconversion and calibration are needed. A student may not connect this sentence to the later residual-image and I/Q mismatch discussion.
fix: With fLO = fRF the image frequency equals fRF, so the image falls on top of the wanted channel and no IF filter can separate them. The receiver therefore downconverts with I and Q paths, and only gain/phase mismatch between them leaves a residual image.

problem: IRR is defined as 'ratio of wanted-signal power to image-signal power at the output'. That ratio equals IRR only when the wanted and image inputs arrive with equal power. The standard definition is the ratio of the conversion gain for the wanted frequency to the conversion gain for the image frequency.
fix: IRR is the ratio of the output power at the wanted frequency to the output power at the image frequency when both inputs have the same power, i.e. the ratio of the two conversion gains. It is stated in dB as IRR = 10 log₁₀(Pwanted/Pimage).

problem: fimage = fRF − 2fIF is quoted without the condition that it must stay positive. A low-side LO needs fRF > 2fIF; otherwise the image falls at a negative frequency (there is no physical image at fLO − fIF) and the design must use a high-side LO instead.
fix: For a low-side LO, fLO = fRF − fIF and fimage = fRF − 2fIF, valid only when fRF > 2fIF. If fRF ≤ 2fIF the image would be at a negative frequency, so a high-side LO is used.

problem: The text says one path gets a 90° phase shift but does not give the sign. With the wrong sign the wanted signal cancels and the image adds — the opposite of what is wanted. Students frequently lose marks on this.
fix: The 90° shift must be applied with the correct sign: shift the path whose LO leads (or lag the other path), so the wanted components add in phase and the image components add in antiphase. The shift is needed at the IF, over the whole band — which is why Hartley needs a wideband 90° phase shifter and Weaver avoids it.

problem: 'It cannot filter sharply at 900 MHz or 2.4 GHz' is too absolute. Fixed SAW and BAW filters at 2 GHz are sharp and are used in phones. The real difficulty is a sharp filter that can be tuned from channel to channel across the band.
fix: A sharp, tunable filter at 900 MHz or 2.4 GHz is hard to build: fixed SAW/BAW filters are sharp but cannot be retuned channel by channel. So the receiver translates the signal to a fixed IF where a cheap, sharp, fixed filter does the channel selection.

problem: The answer says only that 'there is no non-zero IF where an image sits'. The sharper and more standard point is that with fIF = 0 the image frequency equals fRF, so the image cannot be separated from the wanted channel by any filter.
fix: Add: with fLO = fRF, fimage = fRF, so the image coincides with the wanted channel. No filter can remove it; quadrature I/Q downconversion is used, and I/Q gain and phase mismatch then leaves only a residual image plus DC offset.
